title: AI Engineer — Level 4: Expert Depth
description: Serving internals, training dynamics, advanced agent reliability, and the hard trade-offs behind production LLM platforms.

questions.prompt: Standard self-attention is O(n²) in sequence length. Which statement about long-context techniques is most accurate?
options: FlashAttention reduces memory traffic and enables long contexts by tiling and recomputation, but keeps the O(n²) compute; sparse/linear attention variants change the asymptotics at some quality cost
FlashAttention makes attention O(n log n) in compute
RoPE positional encoding removes the quadratic cost entirely
KV caching makes prefill linear in sequence length
questions.answer_notes: FlashAttention is an IO-aware exact algorithm: same O(n²) FLOPs, but avoids materializing the n×n matrix in HBM, so it's memory-bound-faster and enables much longer contexts. Approximate approaches (sliding-window, sparse, linear attention, state-space models) alter the asymptotics but trade recall on long-range dependencies. RoPE handles position representation, not cost; KV cache helps decode, prefill remains quadratic.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Distinguishes real understanding of attention economics from buzzword recall.

questions.prompt: Explain how a modern LLM inference server (vLLM-style) achieves high GPU utilization: cover continuous batching and PagedAttention, and why naive batching fails.
questions.answer_notes: Naive/static batching waits to assemble a batch and holds it until the longest sequence finishes — short requests idle the GPU while long ones run, and padding wastes compute. Continuous batching schedules at the iteration level: each decode step, finished sequences leave and queued ones join, keeping the GPU saturated. PagedAttention manages the KV cache like virtual memory — fixed-size blocks, non-contiguous allocation — eliminating fragmentation and enabling near-full memory use plus prefix sharing across requests. Together they raise throughput several-fold at similar latency. Mention prefill/decode phase separation and chunked prefill as the current frontier.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Serving-infrastructure depth expected for platform-level AI roles.

questions.prompt: Compare RLHF (with PPO) and DPO for preference tuning: how does each work, and why has DPO become popular despite RLHF's flexibility?
questions.answer_notes: RLHF: train a reward model on human preference pairs, then optimize the policy with PPO against it, with a KL penalty to stay near the reference model. Powerful but operationally heavy: four models in memory, RL instability, reward hacking. DPO: derives a closed-form objective showing the policy can be optimized directly on preference pairs (implicitly defining the reward), turning it into a simple classification-style loss — stable, cheap, no reward model or rollouts. Trade-offs: DPO is offline and bounded by the preference dataset; RLHF supports online exploration, process rewards, and richer reward shaping. Follow-ups: KTO/IPO variants, and RLVR (verifiable rewards) for reasoning models.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Post-training literacy at expert level; asked at AI-first companies.

questions.prompt: Your production agent completes 85% of tasks; failures compound across its 10-20 step episodes. Design a reliability program to reach 95%+ — instrumentation, failure taxonomy, and concrete interventions.
questions.answer_notes: Instrument: full trajectory logging (every prompt, tool call, result), per-step and per-episode outcome labels, cost/latency per step. Build a failure taxonomy from sampled failures: wrong plan, wrong tool/arguments, bad tool output unhandled, context overflow/forgetting, premature termination, hallucinated state. Interventions mapped to causes: better tool descriptions and schemas (validation errors fed back), guardrail checks between steps (assertions on invariants), checkpointing + retry from last good state rather than episode restart, context compaction with structured scratchpads, sub-agent decomposition for long tasks, and an eval gym of replayable episodes so every change is A/B-able. Key point: per-step accuracy compounds (0.98^15 ≈ 0.74), so small step-level gains dominate; measure at both granularities.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Real operational agent engineering — the current frontier of senior interviews.

questions.prompt: You quantize a 70B model from BF16 to 4-bit to fit one GPU. Which effect is most likely and most important to verify?
options: Small average benchmark degradation but potentially large regressions on specific capabilities (math, long-tail knowledge, low-resource languages) — so task-specific evals are mandatory
Uniform 50% quality loss across all tasks
No quality change whatsoever, since quantization is lossless
The model's context window shrinks proportionally to bit width
questions.answer_notes: Modern PTQ methods (GPTQ, AWQ, NF4) hold average benchmark scores close to baseline, but degradation is uneven — outlier-heavy layers and precise-recall tasks suffer disproportionately, and generation-quality issues (repetition, subtle reasoning errors) hide behind aggregate scores. Verify on your actual workload evals, not MMLU. Also know: weight-only vs weight+activation (W8A8) quantization, and KV-cache quantization as a separate lever for memory.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Expert-level deployment judgment: knowing where quantization bites.

questions.prompt: Design an internal LLM gateway for a company with 30 product teams: requirements, architecture, and the three hardest problems you'd expect.
questions.answer_notes: Requirements: unified API across providers, authn/z per team, budgets and rate limits, observability (tracing, token accounting), prompt/PII governance, caching, failover. Architecture: a stateless proxy layer with provider adapters; central config for model routing and quotas; async log pipeline to a warehouse for cost attribution and eval mining; response and prefix caching; secrets isolation. Hardest problems: (1) fair rate limiting and cost attribution when providers meter differently (tokens vs requests) and teams share pooled capacity; (2) semantic observability — capturing enough to debug quality without hoarding sensitive data (sampling, redaction, retention); (3) keeping routing/failover from changing behavior — model versions differ, so failover needs per-route eval parity checks, not just liveness. Mention building on open standards and treating the gateway as a product with SLOs.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Platform-scale design; standard for staff/senior platform AI roles.

questions.prompt: In large-model training, what problem does tensor parallelism solve that data parallelism cannot?
options: The model's layers themselves exceed one device's memory, so individual weight matrices must be split across GPUs
The dataset is too large to fit on one machine
Gradients become too noisy with large batch sizes
The learning rate schedule needs per-GPU adjustment
questions.answer_notes: Data parallelism replicates the full model per GPU and shards the batch — it fails once the model itself doesn't fit. Tensor parallelism splits individual matmuls (column/row sharding with all-reduce/all-gather at boundaries) across devices; pipeline parallelism shards by layers with micro-batching to fill bubbles; ZeRO/FSDP shard optimizer state, gradients, and parameters across data-parallel ranks. Real systems compose all of these ('3D parallelism'). Know the communication cost hierarchy: TP needs the fastest interconnect (NVLink domain), PP tolerates slower links.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Expert training-infrastructure knowledge for roles touching model training.

questions.prompt: Architect the safety/guardrail layer for a customer-facing agent that can read user data and execute actions (refunds, account changes). Assume prompt injection will succeed sometimes.
questions.answer_notes: Defense in depth around the assumption of compromise: (1) Least privilege — the agent's tools expose narrow, parameterized operations with server-side authorization checks against the *authenticated user's* permissions, never the model's claims. (2) Deterministic policy enforcement outside the model: irreversible/high-value actions (refund > X) require human confirmation or step-up auth; the LLM can request, not execute. (3) Input hygiene: mark untrusted content, injection classifiers/heuristics on retrieved data. (4) Output controls: schema-constrained actions, moderation on user-visible text. (5) Blast-radius limits: rate/velocity caps per account, anomaly detection, full audit trail, kill switch. (6) Continuous red-teaming with injection corpora in CI. The interviewer wants 'the model is untrusted; the tool boundary is the security boundary' stated explicitly.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Security architecture under adversarial assumptions — expert bar at serious shops.
